name: Sova
headline: Four languages. One musical clock.
standfirst: A Rust live-coding sequencer puts several programming languages on one shared musical timeline. The idea is intriguing; the project still calls itself alpha.
platforms: Windows (maintainer project/build information; not tested here)
evidence: DESK REVIEW / NOT TESTED. Toolglass read the project README and site; no installation, audio run or performance test was conducted.

body.heading: One engine, several ways to think
paragraphs: Sova is a Rust sequencer and musical programming environment designed around a virtual machine for real-time improvisation. Its project README describes four languages—Bob, BaLi, Boinx and Cagire—sharing one VM and I/O layer. The design asks whether musical time can stay stable while a composer moves between different ways of expressing a pattern.

body.heading: A timing system with a large surface area
paragraphs: The maintainers describe a scheduler that looks ahead by roughly 30 milliseconds and a real-time-priority dispatch thread. The project also lists Ableton Link, MIDI, OSC, the Doux audio engine, shader editing and collaborative sessions. These are upstream descriptions, not measurements by Toolglass.

That combination could make Sova feel less like a language with an audio engine attached and more like one instrument with several programming surfaces. The same breadth also creates a substantial engineering and usability challenge.

body.heading: The catch
paragraphs: Sova labels itself active alpha. Toolglass has not checked stability, audio-device support, timing jitter, collaboration recovery or whether the four languages are useful in practice. A musician should treat the feature list as a set of claims to explore, not a guarantee of a finished instrument.

body.heading: A useful first test
paragraphs: Build the desktop client from a pinned revision. Compose the same short eight-bar idea in two languages, confirm both address the same transport, measure MIDI timing under CPU load, then disconnect a second client and observe recovery. That would test the instrument people actually use, not just its README.

verdict: An unusual and potentially fruitful design for live-coded music: several languages share a single sequencer and VM. DESK REVIEW only; Toolglass has not tested it.
nextStep: Try the desktop client and compare one short arrangement across two languages.
